section.title: The Hymn to Wisdom
section.sectionRationale: The dialogue pauses here for one of the most beautiful poems in the Bible. Job (or the narrator through Job) marvels at human ingenuity, miners can tunnel to the ends of the earth for silver, gold, and sapphires, yet no one can mine, buy, or find wisdom that way. Wisdom is hidden from every living thing; only God knows its place. The poem closes with the answer every reader of Job needs: the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom.
section.thesis: Human skill can conquer the deepest mine but not the deepest question; true wisdom is not something we discover by cleverness or purchase with wealth, it is something God alone possesses and graciously discloses, and it comes down finally to reverent trust rather than complete explanation.
section.frameNote: Four movements: a celebration of human ingenuity in mining hidden treasure; the abrupt question of where wisdom itself can be found, since it cannot be mined or bought; wisdom's utter hiddenness from every living creature; and God's own possession of wisdom, disclosed to humanity as the fear of the Lord and turning from evil.

units.label: Mining the depths
units.note: man puts an end to darkness

verses.text: “Surely there is a mine for silver and a place where gold is refined.
Iron is taken from the earth, and copper is smelted from ore.
Man puts an end to the darkness; he probes the farthest recesses for ore in deepest darkness.
Far from human habitation he cuts a shaft in places forgotten by the foot of man. Far from men he dangles and sways.
Food may come from the earth, but from below it is transformed as by fire.
Its rocks are the source of sapphires, containing flecks of gold.
No bird of prey knows that path; no falcon’s eye has seen it.
Proud beasts have never trodden it; no lion has ever prowled over it.
The miner strikes the flint; he overturns mountains at their base.
He hews out channels in the rocks, and his eyes spot every treasure.
He stops up the sources of the streams to bring what is hidden to light.

units.label: But where is wisdom found?
units.note: not in the land of the living

verses.text: But where can {{chokmah|wisdom}} be found, and where does {{tebunah|understanding}} dwell?
No man can know its value, nor is it found in the land of the living.
The ocean depths say, ‘It is not in me,’ while the sea declares, ‘It is not with me.’
It cannot be bought with gold, nor can its price be weighed out in silver.
It cannot be valued in the gold of Ophir, in precious onyx or sapphire.
Neither gold nor crystal can compare to it, nor jewels of fine gold be exchanged for it.
Coral and quartz are unworthy of mention; the price of wisdom is beyond rubies.
Topaz from Cush cannot compare to it, nor can it be valued in pure gold.

units.label: Hidden from every living thing
units.note: Abaddon and Death have only heard a rumor

verses.text: From where then does wisdom come, and where does understanding dwell?
It is hidden from the eyes of every living thing and concealed from the birds of the air.
Abaddon and Death say, ‘We have heard a rumor about it.’

units.label: God alone knows its place
units.note: the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom

verses.text: But God understands its way, and He knows its place.
For He looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens.
When God fixed the weight of the wind and measured out the waters,
when He set a limit for the rain and a path for the thunderbolt,
then He looked at wisdom and appraised it; He established it and searched it out.
And He said to man, ‘Behold, the {{yirah|fear}} of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to {{sur|turn away}} from evil is understanding.’”

chokmah.gloss: Wisdom, the skill of living rightly before God and others. This chapter asks the question that haunts all wisdom literature, where can it be found, and answers that it cannot be mined, bought, or discovered by human effort alone; it must be received from God.

tebunah.gloss: Understanding, insight, discernment, paired with chokmah throughout wisdom literature. The poem asks where it dwells and finds it hidden from every living creature, even the sea and the underworld, until God discloses its place.

yirah.gloss: Fear, reverence, awe. The poem's climactic answer, 'the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom,' identifies the beginning and the sum of wisdom not as intellectual mastery but as reverent, trusting submission to God, echoed throughout Proverbs, Psalms, and Ecclesiastes.

sur.gloss: To turn aside or turn away. Paired with the fear of the Lord, 'to turn away from evil is understanding' completes the poem's definition of wisdom: reverence toward God expressed concretely in turning from wrongdoing, not mere abstract knowledge.

basic.context: This chapter is a pause in the argument, a stand alone poem marveling at how far human skill can reach, miners dig to the ends of the earth for gold and gems, yet asking where wisdom itself can be found. The answer is startling: nowhere on earth, in the sea, or even known fully to death itself. Only God knows wisdom's place, and He has told humanity what it looks like in practice: fearing the Lord and turning from evil.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter functions as the theological center of the whole book. After thirty chapters of confident human argument, both from the friends and from Job, the poem quietly humbles every voice in the dialogue: none of them, however clever, has actually located wisdom. The only wisdom available to humanity is not explanatory mastery of why Job suffers, but reverent trust and obedience.
basic.originalLanguages: The poem searches for chokmah and tebunah, wisdom and understanding, and finds them beyond every human reach, even beyond the sea and the underworld's rumor. God alone possesses and appraises this wisdom, and He gives humanity a concrete definition of it: yirah, the fear of the Lord, and to sur, turn away, from evil.
basic.typology: The chapter's confession that wisdom is hidden from all living things and known only to God anticipates the New Testament's announcement that Christ is the wisdom of God made flesh, in whom all the hidden treasures of wisdom and knowledge are found, no longer merely rumored at by death but revealed in a person.
basic.christ: Job 28 leaves wisdom unreachable by human effort, hidden even from the underworld. The New Testament answers this longing directly: Christ is made unto us wisdom from God, and in Him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, 1 Corinthians 1:30, Colossians 2:3. What this poem could only locate in God's hidden possession is now disclosed in the person of Jesus.
basic.god: God alone knows wisdom's way and place; He is the one who weighed the wind and measured the waters, and having searched wisdom out, He discloses to humanity not an explanation of suffering but a posture: fear Him, and turn from evil. This is God's gracious answer to Job's whole ordeal before the whirlwind speeches even begin.
basic.crossReferences: Proverbs 9:10 and Psalm 111:10 echo the same conclusion, the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. 1 Corinthians 1:24, 30 names Christ as the wisdom of God. Colossians 2:3 says all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ. Ecclesiastes 7:23-24 confesses the same limit on human wisdom that this chapter describes.
basic.oneStory: Job 28 is the book's quiet center: human cleverness can conquer the deepest mine but never wisdom itself, which belongs to God alone and is given to humanity as reverent fear and turning from evil. The Bible's whole story moves toward the moment this hidden wisdom is finally revealed in a person, Jesus Christ, in whom all its treasures are found.

context.literary:
The poem is built on a refrain. Job 28:12 and Job 28:20 ask nearly the same question, 'where can wisdom be found?' and 'from where then does wisdom come?', and they divide the chapter into four parts. Verses 1 to 11 are the miner's part, verses 12 to 19 say what wisdom is worth, verses 20 to 27 say who knows where it is, and verse 28 is the single sentence that speaks to human beings.

The design is a contrast of hands and eyes. In the first part, every verb belongs to a person: he puts an end to darkness, probes, cuts a shaft, overturns mountains, hews channels, stops up streams. The climax is 'his eyes spot every treasure' and he 'brings what is hidden to light.' In the last part, the verbs pass to God, who 'looks to the ends of the earth,' fixed, measured, appraised, established and searched. The one who brings hidden things to light in verse 11 is answered by the One who searched wisdom out in verse 27. Human skill can reach a hidden treasure, but only God can reach a hidden wisdom.

There is also a small chorus of voices. Bird and beast cannot find the path, verses 7 and 8. The ocean depths and the sea speak, saying 'It is not in me,' verse 14. Abaddon and Death speak, saying they have heard a rumor, verse 22. Only at the end does God speak, and He says something that can be done. The list of who does not know builds toward the person who does.

The chapter has no 'I' and no 'you.' Unlike the speeches on either side of it, it addresses no opponent, a calm room between the storm of Job's oath in chapter 27 and the storm of his lament in chapter 29.
context.historical:
The opening lines describe real ancient industry, and the first readers would have recognised it. Israel's own land was praised as one 'whose rocks are iron and whose hills are ready to be mined for copper,' Deuteronomy 8:9, and copper was mined and smelted in the Arabah and the Sinai by people who dug shafts into rock. The strange phrase of verse 4, in which the miner 'dangles and sways' far from human habitation, seems to describe just such a man swinging in a shaft.

The treasures named in the second part were the finest trade goods of the day. Ophir was a source of gold for Solomon's fleet, 1 Kings 10:11, Cush is a region of the upper Nile, as the BSB footnote says, and onyx, sapphire and topaz were among the stones on the high priest's breastplate, Exodus 28:17-20. The poet chooses the most valuable things his hearers could imagine in order to say that none of them will buy wisdom.

Wisdom, in the ancient Near East, was a craft of living well that scribes and sages taught, and every court prized it. Israel had its own school of sages, and in it wisdom was tied to the fear of the LORD, Proverbs 1:7 and Psalm 111:10. The poem speaks into that world. It affirms human skill in the mine and rejects the idea that skill alone reaches wisdom.

The date of the poem cannot be fixed. Its language and themes are close to Proverbs 1 to 9 and Ecclesiastes, which is why some place it in the age of Solomon or later. The book sets Job in a patriarchal age, and the poet has given the poem to a speaker in that age, whatever the date of its composition.
context.canonical:
Job 28 stands in a family of texts that ask where wisdom comes from. Proverbs 8 is its nearest relative: wisdom cries out in the streets, says she was there when God 'inscribed a circle on the face of the deep,' Proverbs 8:27, and is more precious than rubies, Proverbs 8:11. Job says no one can find her. Proverbs says she calls out to be found. Both can be true, because in Job it is human searching that fails, and in Proverbs it is God's invitation that succeeds. Proverbs 2:4-6 joins the two: seek her like silver and hidden treasure, yet 'the LORD gives wisdom.'

The end of the poem is quoted almost word for word in the wisdom literature: 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom,' Proverbs 9:10, Psalm 111:10 and Proverbs 1:7. Ecclesiastes ends on the same note, 'Fear God and keep His commandments,' Ecclesiastes 12:13, after confessing that wisdom was 'beyond me,' Ecclesiastes 7:23-24. Deuteronomy answers the search from another side: the word 'is not in heaven' nor 'beyond the sea,' but 'very near you,' Deuteronomy 30:12-14.

The New Testament picks the poem up. Paul closes his hymn of awe with 'O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God,' Romans 11:33. In 1 Corinthians 1:20-30 he asks where the wise man is, and answers that Christ has become wisdom from God for us. Colossians 2:3 says all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Him, which is the mine of Job 28 with a name on it. James 1:5 finishes the thought: wisdom cannot be bought, but God 'gives generously to all without finding fault.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author sets a still poem in the middle of a loud argument to change the question. Twenty-seven chapters have asked why Job suffers. This chapter asks something else: what would it mean to understand it? The answer is that no amount of ingenuity can produce such understanding, that the whole created order holds no path to it, and that the one who has it has chosen to say something practical to us and not something explanatory.

For the first hearers, the poem was a call to humility and a redefinition of wisdom. The friends thought wisdom was the ability to name the cause of suffering. Job thought it was the ability to demand a hearing. The poem removes both by making wisdom a possession of God and a gift in the form of a way of life. The definition is uncomfortably close to how the book introduced its hero, 'fearing God and shunning evil,' Job 1:1. The reader is meant to notice that Job already lives what the poem calls wisdom, and that the friends' clever certainty is what is missing. The chapter also prepares for the end. When God finally speaks, He will not explain. He will reveal Himself, and the poem has taught the reader to expect it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The poem does not condemn human achievement. The description of the mine is admiring, and mining, smelting and craft are treated as gifts. Nothing in the chapter tells a believer to distrust learning, science or hard work. What it records is the limit: no skill, however great, reaches the wisdom that sees the whole of life as God sees it.

What it prescribes is in its last verse. The fear of the Lord and turning from evil are what God has told us to do. That is practical and obedience-shaped. It should not be turned into a slogan to silence someone who is hurting. Job's friends would have loved to answer his agony with 'Just fear God.' The chapter gives that line to God to say to people, and it does not hand it to us as a way of ending honest questions. The right use is to seek wisdom by asking God, James 1:5, and to keep living in reverence and integrity while the answers are still hidden.

debates.question: Who speaks this chapter, Job or the narrator?

views.label: Job's own words
views.case: The chapter is presented within Job's ongoing discourse, following directly from chapter 27 with no new speech heading, so many read it as Job's own meditation.

views.label: A narrator's interlude
views.case: Others note the poem's calm, resolved tone differs so much from Job's surrounding anguish that it may function as an authorial aside, stepping outside the dialogue to comment on it, similar to a chorus in Greek drama.

debates.bearing: Either way, the poem's message stands independently: none of the human speakers in the book, including Job, has actually found wisdom, which is exactly the point the chapter makes.

debates.question: Does 'the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom' answer the problem of Job's suffering, or evade it?

views.label: An evasion, deferring the real question
views.case: Some feel this answer, like Bildad's, sidesteps Job's specific complaint about undeserved suffering rather than resolving it.

views.label: The book's deliberate, honest answer
views.case: Given that God's own speeches in 38-41 will confirm this same point, that reverent trust rather than full explanation is the appropriate human response, this chapter previews and legitimizes the book's actual resolution rather than evading it.

debates.bearing: The second reading fits the flow of the whole book: chapter 28 quietly anticipates what God's appearance from the whirlwind will confirm at far greater length.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond the names of wisdom and understanding, several small features hold the poem together. The first is the repeated word 'place.' The Hebrew maqom appears in verse 1 for the place where gold is refined, in verse 6 for the place of sapphires, and in the refrains of verses 12 and 20, where understanding has a place, and in verse 23 where God knows 'its place.' The miner knows every place, and God alone knows this one. The word for 'way,' derekh, is set beside it in verse 23, where God understands its way and its place, as if wisdom were something to be located on a map.

The second is the verb behind 'understands.' Verse 23 says God hevin its way. That is the causative form of bin, the root of tebunah, understanding. The poem uses the noun in the refrain and the verb in the answer, so that understanding is found only in the one who does the understanding. Human beings receive tebunah as a gift, but God is the source of the discerning itself.

The third is the four verbs of verse 27. 'He looked at wisdom and appraised it; He established it and searched it out.' The verb the BSB renders 'appraised' is one that elsewhere means to count or recount, so the line can be read as He saw it and declared it. 'Searched it out' comes from the root of investigation that lies behind the noun in Job 5:9 and Job 9:10, where God's works are 'unsearchable' and 'beyond searching out.' The One whose works cannot be searched is here the One who searched wisdom. And the BSB footnote on verse 11 notes that the Greek and Latin read 'searches' where the Hebrew has 'stops up,' a reminder that the mining verses are hard to translate.

The fourth is the word for jewels. The poem says the price of wisdom is beyond rubies, using the Hebrew peninim, and Proverbs 3:15 and 8:11 use the same word in the same claim, as though the sages were quoting one another.

The fifth is in the last verse. The BSB prints 'the Lord' in small letters rather than LORD, signalling the divine title Adonai and not the covenant name, and 'to man' is the general word for humankind. The two phrases 'fear' and 'turn away from evil' are exactly the pair used to describe Job in Job 1:1, and the verb translated 'turn away' is the same one as 'shunning.' Wisdom, as the poem defines it, is Job's own way of life.

typology.type: The hidden treasure that can only be found by revelation, Job 28:12-23
typology.fulfillment: Job's poem says wisdom is hidden from every living thing and that no price can buy it. Jesus tells of a treasure hidden in a field that a man finds and buys with everything he has, Matthew 13:44, and Paul says that in Christ 'are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,' Colossians 2:3. The mine has become a person. The correspondence is real, but the direction changes: in Job people dig for treasure, and in the gospel the hidden treasure comes to the finder as a gift, since the Son 'has made Him known,' John 1:18. The parable goes further than the poem, which offers no purchase at all.

typology.type: Wisdom that God appraised and established, Job 28:27
typology.fulfillment: Before the world was made, wisdom stood beside God, Proverbs 8:22-31, and the New Testament names the Son as the one through whom all things were created and hold together, Colossians 1:16-17, and as the Word who was with God in the beginning, John 1:1-3. Job 28:27 shows God looking at wisdom as He sets the wind's weight and the waters' measure. The type points to Christ as the wisdom of God who orders the world and redeems it. It is a pattern, not a proof: Proverbs personifies wisdom as a poetic figure, and the New Testament gives that figure a face.

typology.type: Death and Abaddon who have only heard a rumor, Job 28:22
typology.fulfillment: The realm of the dead knows wisdom only by report. In the last book of the Bible, Abaddon is the name of the angel of the Abyss, Revelation 9:11, and Christ, the Living One who died, says 'I hold the keys of Death and of Hades,' Revelation 1:18. The place that could only whisper about wisdom is opened by the one who is wisdom. The type does not match in detail, since Job speaks of the underworld as ignorant, not as a domain that a saviour enters, but its direction is clear.

typology.type: The price that cannot be paid in silver and gold, Job 28:15-19
typology.fulfillment: The poem removes every currency: gold, silver, onyx, sapphire, coral, rubies, topaz. Peter says believers were redeemed 'not with perishable things such as silver or gold' but with 'the precious blood of Christ,' 1 Peter 1:18-19, and Isaiah invites those 'without money' to buy 'without cost,' Isaiah 55:1. What cannot be bought is given. The pattern is reversed in the gospel, where the price is paid by someone else, so the type falls short of showing that costly grace.

study.christ:
Job 28 does not name the Messiah, and it is safer to say what it leaves open than what it predicts. It says wisdom is the possession of God, that no human being can locate it, and that God has told us what a wise life looks like. Each of those three statements has a New Testament fulfilment.

The first is that wisdom is personal in God's hands. In Proverbs 8:22-31 wisdom speaks as a craftsman at God's side before creation, and the New Testament identifies the Son as the one 'through whom all things were created,' Colossians 1:16, whose person the church calls the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24. The Christ who was 'the power of God and the wisdom of God' is the answer to where wisdom dwells. He is not a rumor at the edge of Sheol but the presence at the Father's side.

The second is that Christ is the one who reveals what no digging could reach. 'No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son... has made Him known,' John 1:18. Jesus praised the Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to little children, and said no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom He chooses to reveal Him, Matthew 11:25-27. That is the poem's structure turned into a promise. What the depths and the sea could not say, the Son does. And 'in Him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,' Colossians 2:3, so the mine that no bird has seen is a person who invites us to come.

The third is that the definition of wisdom is seen in Him. The promised Messiah is described as the one on whom rests 'the Spirit of wisdom and understanding' and 'fear of the LORD,' in whom He delights, Isaiah 11:2-3, the same pair the poem sets side by side. Jesus 'grew in wisdom,' Luke 2:52, and was heard because of His reverence, Hebrews 5:7. The one who lived the fear of the LORD without failing is the wisdom that the poem said could not be found.

This matters for the Christian reading of the poem. Paul does not say the cross explains everything. He says that to those who are called, 'Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God,' 1 Corinthians 1:24, is a person and not a theory. The suffering Job could not explain is met by a wisdom that enters suffering, and the wise man who asked 'where is wisdom?' is answered at Golgotha.
study.god:
The God of this poem is the one who knows. Where the miner sees a single seam, God 'looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything under the heavens.' His knowledge is not gathered by effort. He sees, and the seeing is complete. Job 28 gives a theology of divine omniscience that is at once vast and unthreatening, for the point is not that God watches us but that He knows the way of what we cannot find.

He is also the Creator who measured and set limits. He 'fixed the weight of the wind,' 'measured out the waters,' 'set a limit for the rain and a path for the thunderbolt.' These are small, intimate tasks for a great God, and they reach even to weather. His wisdom is displayed in the details of creation, and in Psalm 135:7 the same tasks are a reason for praise. The verses also put wisdom in relation to creation: He looked at wisdom while He measured. Wisdom is not a thing He made. It is the mind with which He made, and that is why it cannot be purchased by anyone.

There is a tension the poem holds. Wisdom is hidden, and yet God speaks. The whole chapter denies that the sea, the birds, the living or the dead can find it, and then a last verse begins, 'And He said to man.' God is hidden and God is communicative. The hiddenness is not a barrier but a preparation, so that when God speaks, people know that what they have is a gift. The Bible does this in many places, and Deuteronomy 29:29 puts it in a sentence: the secret things belong to the LORD, but the things revealed belong to us.

What God tells us is short. 'The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.' The God who knows everything gives us a task that fits in a sentence. That fits His character. He is not withholding an explanation to tease us. He is giving us what we need to live, and what we need is Him, reverently trusted.

For worship, the poem calls us to stop trying to buy or dig our way into the mind of God and to bow before it. The right response to a God whose ways we cannot trace is the one Paul makes: awe, and a song, Romans 11:33-36.

crossReferences.note: Wisdom speaks as one who stood beside God before the world was made, rejoicing in His presence. It fills in what Job 28:27 says briefly, that God looked at wisdom and established it, and shows why no created thing could tell where she lives.

To seek wisdom as silver and hidden treasure is to discern the fear of the LORD, and 'the LORD gives wisdom.' It joins the two halves of Job 28, the searching and the gift, and shows they belong together.

Wisdom is better than silver and gold and more precious than rubies, and by her the LORD founded the earth. It is the positive side of Job's list of unbuyable jewels, and it explains why the poem places wisdom next to creation.

Job is described as blameless and upright, fearing God and shunning evil. The final verse of Job 28 uses these very words as the definition of wisdom, so the poem quietly says that the man the friends condemn already has what they lack.

The Teacher tested everything by wisdom, and it was beyond him, out of reach and very deep. It confesses the same limit as Job 28:12-14 from the side of a searcher, and makes the two books companions on the humility of the wise.

The word is not in heaven or beyond the sea, but very near, in the mouth and heart. It answers Job 28:14 with revelation: what could not be found has been given, so the sea's 'It is not with me' is met by a God who speaks.

Paul sings of the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, with unsearchable judgments and untraceable ways. He gives the awe of Job 28 a doxology, because from Him and through Him and to Him are all things.

Paul asks where the wise man is, and says God made the world's wisdom foolish and that Christ has become wisdom from God for believers. It is Job 28 answered: wisdom cannot be discovered by the world's cleverness and is found in a crucified Christ.

Paul's language of hidden treasure is the miner's language, and here the mine has a name and a face. It shows that the search the poem describes ends in a person, and that the knowing of Him is meant for hearts knit together in love.
If any lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault. It is the practical side of the poem: wisdom cannot be bought with gold, but it is given to those who ask.

study.oneStory:
Job 28 belongs to a conversation that begins in Eden. The tree was 'desirable for obtaining wisdom,' Genesis 3:6, and the woman took it. Humanity has tried ever since to lay hold of wisdom without God, by cleverness, by wealth, by mastery of the earth, and the poem in Job 28 is the honest audit of what that reaches. It reaches the deepest mine and the farthest star. It does not reach the point of things.

The Bible then tells how God hands wisdom back. He gives Israel a law that shows their 'wisdom and understanding in the sight of the peoples,' Deuteronomy 4:6, and He gives Solomon a discerning heart, 1 Kings 3:9-12. The sages of Proverbs teach that it begins with the fear of the LORD. But the sages also say that wisdom itself keeps out of reach, Ecclesiastes 7:23-24, and Israel's history keeps showing that a nation with the law can still lose the wisdom.

The answer comes in Jesus. He is the one greater than Solomon, Matthew 12:42, the Word through whom all things were made, and the hidden treasure that has been found. At the cross the world's wisdom failed to recognise Him, 1 Corinthians 2:7-8, and what looked like foolishness turned out to be the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24. The Spirit of wisdom rests on Him, Isaiah 11:2, and He gives it to those who ask, James 1:5.

The end of the story completes the poem. Heaven's song is 'Worthy is the Lamb, who was slain, to receive power and riches and wisdom,' Revelation 5:12. And 'the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water,' Isaiah 11:9. The sea that said 'It is not in me' is filled with the knowledge it could not give, and the people who searched by lamp in the dark will know as they are known, in the light of the face of the God who alone understood the way to wisdom.

sermon.title: Job: Wrestling with Suffering
sermon.why: Piper's sermon on Job 2:11-31:40 directly quotes this chapter as one of its five summary lessons, citing 28:12-13 and 23, 'where shall wisdom be found... man does not know the way to it... God understands the way to it, and he knows its place,' as evidence that wisdom behind Job's suffering is real but hidden from human view.

quiz.q: What contrast does the poem draw in verses 1-11 and 12-19?

options.text: Human skill can mine the earth's deepest treasures, but it cannot mine, buy, or find wisdom itself.
options.note: The elaborate mining description in verses 1-11 sets up the abrupt question in verse 12, 'where can wisdom be found.'

options.text: Mining shows impressive human skill, and the poem values wisdom as ultimately even more precious.
options.note: Close, this captures part of the contrast, but understates the sharper point that wisdom cannot be found by mining methods at all, not merely that it is more valuable.

options.text: Wisdom is easier to find than silver or gold.
options.note: The poem says the opposite; wisdom cannot be found by any of the same methods that locate precious metals.

options.text: There is no real difference between wisdom and wealth.
options.note: The whole point of the contrast is that wisdom cannot be measured or bought like wealth.

quiz.q: Where does the poem say wisdom can ultimately be found?

options.text: Only with God, who alone understands its way and knows its place.
options.note: Verses 23-27 are explicit: God alone possesses this wisdom.

options.text: In the depths of the sea.
options.note: Verse 14 has the sea itself deny having it.

options.text: Among the dead in Sheol.
options.note: Verse 22 says Abaddon and Death have only 'heard a rumor,' not full possession of it.

options.text: In the deep order of creation itself, distilled from long human reflection.
options.note: Close in spirit, wisdom does relate to creation's order, but the poem is explicit that only God, not human reflection alone, actually knows wisdom's place.

quiz.q: What is the chapter's final definition of wisdom in verse 28?

options.text: The fear of the Lord, and turning away from evil.
options.note: This is the poem's climactic and explicit conclusion.

options.text: Owning as much gold and silver as possible.
options.note: The whole poem argues wisdom cannot be measured in wealth.

options.text: Successfully explaining why the righteous suffer.
options.note: The poem deliberately withholds this kind of explanatory wisdom, offering reverence and obedience instead.

options.text: A deep intellectual understanding of the world's mysteries.
options.note: Close, wisdom does involve real understanding, but verse 28 defines it specifically as reverent fear of God and turning from evil, not mastery of creation's secrets.

quiz.q: How does this chapter anticipate the New Testament?

options.text: It anticipates Christ, in whom all the hidden treasures of wisdom and knowledge are finally disclosed.
options.note: Colossians 2:3 and 1 Corinthians 1:30 directly answer the hiddenness of wisdom described here.

options.text: It teaches that wisdom remains hidden from humanity in this life, with no resolution offered.
options.note: Close to the Old Testament tension the poem raises, but the New Testament specifically announces this very wisdom has now been revealed in Christ.

options.text: It has no connection to anything in the New Testament.
options.note: It is one of the clearest Old Testament anticipations of Christ as the wisdom of God.

options.text: It proves that human effort will eventually locate wisdom on its own.
options.note: The poem insists the opposite, that wisdom must be disclosed by God, not discovered by unaided human effort.

quiz.q: Why does this chapter function as a pause in the surrounding dialogue?

options.text: It steps back from the heated arguments to confess that none of the speakers, friends or Job, has actually located wisdom.
options.note: Its calm, meditative tone and universal scope set it apart from the personal accusations surrounding it.

options.text: It resolves every question raised earlier in the book.
options.note: It offers a posture, fearing God, rather than resolving the specific question of why Job suffers.

options.text: It agrees with the friends that human wisdom is real and valuable, without necessarily endorsing their specific theology.
options.note: Close, the poem does treat wisdom as genuinely valuable, but its main point is to humble every human claim to have found it, including the friends' confident doctrine of retribution.

options.text: It has no relationship to the surrounding chapters at all.
options.note: It functions as a deliberate interlude commenting on the futility of the preceding arguments.

questions: The poem marvels at human skill reaching into the deepest mine, yet unable to reach wisdom itself. Where in your own life have you relied on skill or cleverness to solve something that actually requires humility before God?
Wisdom, the chapter says, cannot be bought with any treasure. Are there things you have tried to purchase, through effort, achievement, or money, that can really only be received as a gift from God?

The chapter's final answer to a book full of hard questions is simply, fear the Lord and turn from evil. How does that simple, practical wisdom sit with you when you want a fuller explanation for your own suffering?
Wisdom was hidden from every living thing until God disclosed it; now it is revealed fully in Christ. How has knowing Jesus given you access to wisdom you could never have found on your own?

This chapter interrupts a long, heated argument with quiet reflection. What would it look like for you to pause an anxious or angry train of thought this week and simply return to reverent fear of God?

translationNotes.note: 'A mine for silver' begins an extended description of ancient mining, some of the most detailed technical poetry in the Hebrew Bible, underscoring the height of human ingenuity before the poem pivots to what lies beyond it.
'Abaddon and Death' are personified here as beings who have heard only a rumor of wisdom, emphasizing that not even the realm beyond life has full access to it, only God does.
This verse is widely regarded as the theological summary not only of Job but of Israel's whole wisdom tradition, closely paralleling Proverbs 1:7 and 9:10, and Psalm 111:10.
